title: Sharding — Flashcards
subtitle: 36 cards across 8 categories · Click to flip · Export to Anki / Quizlet

cards.a: Splitting data across multiple independent machines, each with its own CPU, memory, and storage. Together all shards form the complete dataset.
Splitting a large table into smaller logical pieces within a single database instance. No new machines — just better organization.
Splitting rows across partitions. Same columns, fewer rows per partition.
Splitting columns across partitions. All rows present, but each partition holds a different subset of columns.
The field used to decide which shard a record belongs to. The most important sharding decision — a bad shard key causes hotspots and expensive queries.
When one shard handles far more traffic than others, becoming a bottleneck that negates the benefit of sharding.
A hot spot caused by inherently popular keys — not bad distribution. A celebrity's shard gets 1000x more requests than a normal user's shard.
A query that needs data from multiple shards. Requires contacting all relevant shards, waiting for all responses, then merging results — expensive.
The shard key should have many unique values so data can be spread across many shards. A boolean key (2 values) can only ever produce 2 shards.
Values of the shard key should spread roughly evenly across shards so no single shard gets overloaded.
The shard key should match your most common query patterns so those queries hit just one shard instead of fanning out to all of them.

cards.q: Why created_at is a bad shard key
cards.a: All new writes go to the shard holding the most recent time range — a constant write hotspot. Older shards sit mostly idle.

cards.q: Why a boolean is a bad shard key
cards.a: Only 2 possible values = only 2 shards max. Distribution is almost always uneven (e.g., 90% free users vs 10% premium).
Records are assigned to shards based on continuous ranges of the shard key (e.g., user IDs 1–1M go to shard 1). Simple, supports range scans, but prone to hotspots.
A hash function determines which shard a record goes to (e.g., shard = hash(user_id) % N). The default strategy — produces even distribution across shards.
A lookup table explicitly maps each record to its shard. Maximum flexibility, but every request needs a directory lookup and the directory is a single point of failure.
A technique that minimizes data movement when shards are added or removed. Only ~1/N of data needs to move instead of nearly all of it with simple modulo hashing.

cards.q: Best use case for range-based sharding
cards.a: Multi-tenant SaaS systems where each company queries only its own range of IDs. Different tenants naturally hit different shards.

cards.q: Downside of simple modulo hash sharding
cards.a: Adding or removing a shard changes the modulo, causing almost every record to map to a different shard — massive data movement required.
A distributed transaction protocol: coordinator asks all shards to 'prepare', then tells them to 'commit'. Guarantees atomicity but is slow and fragile — a crash mid-way can leave the system stuck.

Coordinating multi-shard operations as a sequence of independent steps, each with a compensating action. If step 3 fails, compensating actions undo steps 1 and 2. Achieves eventual consistency without 2PC.
A step that undoes a previously completed operation if a later step in a saga fails. Example: if adding funds to User B fails, refund User A.

cards.q: Best way to avoid distributed transactions
cards.a: Choose a shard key that keeps all data involved in a transaction on the same shard. Single-shard transactions are fast and need no coordination.
Storing copies of related data on the same shard to avoid cross-shard joins. Trades data duplication and update complexity for faster, single-shard reads.
Combining two fields as the shard key (e.g., hash(user_id + date)) to spread a hot user's data across multiple shards over time.
Expensive global queries (e.g., top trending posts) are run once against all shards and the result is cached. Subsequent requests hit the cache instead of fanning out.
Uses a partitioner (e.g., Murmur3) with virtual nodes — a form of consistent hashing that maps partition keys to token ranges on nodes.
Hashes the partition key to route items to internal partitions and automatically splits/merges partitions as data grows. The internals are not exposed to users.
Uses range-based chunks with a background balancer that automatically splits and migrates chunks to keep shards balanced. Not classic ring-based consistent hashing.
An open-source sharding layer for MySQL. Handles query routing, cross-shard operations, and online resharding. Resharding is operator-driven, not automatic.

cards.q: When to introduce sharding in an interview
cards.a: Only after establishing a bottleneck: storage limits, write throughput a single DB can't handle, or read load exceeding even read replicas. Do the math first.
Proposing sharding before proving it's necessary. Slow down, do the capacity math, confirm a single database can't handle the load.
A design problem — likely the wrong shard key. Common queries should hit one shard. If they don't, reconsider your shard key, denormalize, or precompute.
Hash-based sharding with consistent hashing on a high-cardinality key aligned to your access patterns (e.g., user_id for user-centric apps).
